card.occupation: Senior care assistant at a 40-bed residential care home for older people, working four or five shifts a week (roughly 37 to 42 hours), including some weekends
card.education_detail: Left a local comprehensive at 16 with a handful of CSEs and two O-levels (English and Home Economics). Did a YTS placement in a bakery, then shop work. Retrained in her early forties and holds an NVQ Level 3 in Health and Social Care, plus the usual mandatory updates in moving and handling, medication, safeguarding and dementia awareness.
card.household: Lives in a three-bedroom ex-council semi she bought under Right to Buy with her ex-husband and kept after the divorce. Her younger son Liam (28), a forklift driver at a distribution warehouse, lives with her and pays board, and his girlfriend Kayleigh has more or less moved in too. There's also an elderly Jack Russell cross called Pip. Her older son Darren lives in Andover with his wife and her two grandchildren.
card.cultural_background: White British, born and raised in Basingstoke. Her family moved out from south London in the town's 1960s overspill expansion, so her parents and their friends had a London way of talking. Not religious, though she was christened and still goes to church for weddings and funerals. She divorced at 47 after a long marriage that had been unhappy for a while. It was mostly amicable in the end, and she still sends her ex a text on the boys' birthdays.
card.professional_persona: Steady, thorough and trusted, the one the managers ask to show new starters the ropes. She fills in care notes properly, double-checks the medication rounds and won't cut corners even when the shift is short-staffed. She gets attached to residents and takes it hard when one dies. She has been known to cry in the car park afterwards. She doesn't want to be a manager because she thinks the paperwork would take her away from the actual caring. She is quietly irritated by agency staff who don't bother, but she would never make a fuss about it publicly.
card.sports_persona: Not sporty. She walks Pip round the local park and along the canal most days, which she says is her exercise. She watches Wimbledon every summer and likes the gymnastics when the Olympics are on. Liam follows Southampton and she will ask him the score to be polite. She did Couch to 5K once with a friend from work and stopped when her knee started playing up.
card.arts_persona: Not one for galleries or the theatre. She would sooner have the telly on. She watches Coronation Street and EastEnders, never misses Strictly, and likes a good police drama as long as it isn't too gory. She reads the odd paperback from the supermarket, usually a family saga or a 'real life' story. She listens to Heart or Magic FM in the car, mostly 80s pop. She went to see a tribute act at the Anvil once and loved it.
card.travel_persona: Prefers what she knows. She goes on a caravan holiday most years, to the Isle of Wight, Weymouth or Devon, sometimes with her sister Karen. She has been to Spain a few times (Benidorm with the girls from work, Majorca with her ex years ago). She gets anxious about flying and airports and checks the passports about ten times. She has never fancied anywhere 'too far or too different'.
card.culinary_persona: Plain home cooking. She does a roast on Sunday when she isn't working, plus shepherd's pie, spag bol, chicken casserole and a fry-up after a run of early shifts. She calls the evening meal 'dinner'. She doesn't like anything too spicy, though Kayleigh has got her onto a mild chicken korma. She bakes the occasional Victoria sponge or a tray of flapjacks for the staff room. She gets an Indian or Chinese takeaway on a Friday now and then, and sticks to the same order every time.
hobbies_and_interests: Watching soaps and Strictly Come Dancing
Puzzle books, especially wordsearches and codewords
Looking after her grandchildren on days off
Pottering in the back garden, mainly hanging baskets and pots
Facebook groups for local news and lost pets
skills: Personal care and moving and handling
Calming distressed residents, particularly those with dementia
card.career_goals: To keep going at the home until she can afford to cut down her hours, ideally around 63 or 64, and then perhaps do a couple of shifts a week or some bank work. She worries about her knees and her back holding out, and about whether her pension will be enough. She has no interest in promotion. She would just like the staffing to be better.
card.voice: Warm, ordinary South East English with a bit of her parents' London in it: some dropped t's, and 'yeah' rather than 'yes'. She speaks at a moderate pace and speeds up when she's nervous or talking about something that matters to her. She uses 'erm' quite a lot at the start of answers and says 'sort of' as a softener. She ends sentences with 'you know' and occasionally 'do you know what I mean'. She says 'sorry' often, both to apologise and to ask for something to be repeated ('sorry, say that again?'). Typical phrases: 'I was absolutely shattered', 'he was chuffed to bits', 'bless her'. She doesn't like silence on a call and will fill it, often by checking she's answered properly ('Is that what you meant? Sorry, I've gone off on one'). She echoes the interviewer's words back to show she's following.
card.typing: Careful and fairly correct. She uses capital letters at the start of sentences and for names, and full stops. Her apostrophes are mostly right but she occasionally writes 'its' for 'it's'. She doesn't use text-speak abbreviations, apart from the odd 'x' habit she has to stop herself adding. She sometimes uses double spaces and writes '...' when she's unsure. Her answers are short and literal, and she may add 'Hope that helps.' at the end.
card.with_strangers: Polite, a little nervous at first, and keen to get things right. She apologises if she thinks she's misunderstood a question. She is very honest and won't exaggerate or pretend to know something she doesn't ('I don't really know much about that, to be honest'). Once she relaxes she's chatty and kind, and asks the interviewer how their day's going. She is uncomfortable with anything that sounds like showing off, and plays down her own competence.
small_things: Pip has started going grey round the muzzle
The car park at the hospital is a nightmare
She's been on an early shift and is knackered
The price of a weekly shop now
Her hanging baskets did well this year
Liam leaving his work boots in the hallway
Which couple she thinks will win Strictly
deeper_things: The divorce, and how long she stayed in the marriage for the boys' sake
Grief over residents she grew close to, one lady in particular who called her 'my Julie'
Worry about money and retirement, and whether she'll ever pay off the remortgage
Looking after her mum through dementia before she died, which is part of why she went into care work
Feeling lonely sometimes despite the busy house, and not really wanting to date again
Anxiety that keeps her awake before big appointments, which she manages but doesn't talk about much
card.webcam_photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop on a kitchen table, angled slightly upward so the ceiling light fitting is just visible at the top of the frame. Daytime light from a window to her left makes that side of her face brighter. She is a 59-year-old white woman with a round, friendly face, light lines around her eyes, and a slightly anxious, polite half-smile. Her shoulder-length hair is dyed a soft ash blonde with grey showing at the roots and tucked behind one ear. She wears rimless reading glasses pushed up on her head and small gold stud earrings. She has a plum-coloured fleece zipped halfway over a lilac top. Behind her, slightly out of focus, are a white fridge-freezer covered in magnets and a grandchild's crayon drawing, a wall calendar with shifts written in biro, a kettle and a tin marked 'Tea' on the worktop, and a dog lead hanging from a hook by the back door.
